title: Jake Bauers named NLCS MVP as Brewers advance to World Series after sweeping Dodgers - CBS Sports
description: Bauers is the first Brewers LCS MVP, despite the team winning the pennant in 1982
body:
Bauers is the first Brewers LCS MVP, despite the team winning the pennant in 1982
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:34 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Milwaukee Brewers have won the 2026 National League pennant. They swept the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers with a 6-4 win in Game 4 Thursday night in Game 4. The NLCS MVP is Jake Bauers and it's one heck of a story. We'll get to that. Bauers went 4 for 14 in the series, but he made his hits count. He doubled in two runs to cut the Dodgers' lead in half in Game 4 and had the big blow in Game 3 with a go-ahead, two-run home run in the seventh inning. He had six RBI in the four-game series and that doesn't even include the impact he had in Game 2 with a 12-pitch walk in the third inning that helped chase 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto from the game. "There was never a doubt in that dugout what was going to happen," Bauers said after the game. "We knew we were going to win."An interesting twist here is that this is the first LCS MVP for the Brewers franchise. They won the American League pennant in 1982, but the MVP in that ALCS went to a player from the losing Angels: Fred Lynn, who went a ridiculous 11 for 18 (.611) with two doubles, a home run and five RBI in the five-game series. He was easily the best player in the series, but it still sounds weird to have a player from the losing team to be named the most valuable player in the series. 
There was no such worry in this series. The Brewers thoroughly dominated the Dodgers in every facet of the game. They had more than a handful of the most valuable players in the series. Arguments could have been made for William Contreras and Aaron Ashby. Robert Gasser was outstanding in his five scoreless innings in Game 3. JoJo Romero and DL Hall were great. Jackson Chourio hit a huge homer. Garrett Mitchell hit two. David Hamilton was 4 for 7 with a home run. Christian Yelich was good. As for Bauers, he's floated through seven different organizations and nearly retired after the 2023 season, but continued his career because his then-pregnant wife needed health insurance. He spent time in the minors and majors in 2025. This season, he had a breakout, hitting .266/.389/.484 (140 OPS+) with 22 doubles, 26 homers, 86 RBI, 93 runs and 3.3 WAR. 
And now he's the NLCS MVP.

title: Tarik Skubal free agency: What Dodgers ace said after playoff elimination - CBS Sports
description: The two-time Cy Young winner hits the market this offseason in a winter of insecurity surrounding the looming CBA
body:
The two-time Cy Young winner hits the market this offseason in a winter of insecurity surrounding the looming CBA negotiations
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 16, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:28 am ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Ace left-hander Tarik Skubal watched his Dodgers get eliminated in the NLCS from the dugout in Game 4 on Thursday night. Now, Skubal's next stop is free agency this coming offseason. He will be the top free agent on the market and command an absurd amount of money before signing on the dotted line. Unsurprisingly, Skubal didn't have much to say on the matter after Game 4. "I'm not going to comment on my future really at all," he said, via MLB.com. "Today sucks, you know, and that's kind of where my head's at."Skubal heads to free agency having made the playoffs for three straight years and posted a 2.13 ERA in eight playoff starts, but his teams have been unable to make the World Series. In fact, the trip to the NLCS this year with the Dodgers was the deepest he's ever been in the playoffs. The Tigers made the ALDS in both 2024 and 2025 before being eliminated. The 29-year-old Skubal was the American League Cy Young winner in both 2024 and 2025. This season, he suffered an injury to his pitching elbow that required surgery, a new procedure called NanoScope surgery. He healed remarkably quickly, only missing starts between April 29 and June 13. 
Nine starts later and the Tigers -- despite only being 2 ½ games out of a playoff spot -- decided to get in front of missing the postseason and losing Skubal to free agency. They traded him to the Dodgers at the deadline for a package that included top prospect Zyhir Hope. Between the two teams this season, Skubal made 26 starts and went 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA (155 ERA+), 0.96 WHIP and 186 strikeouts in 158 ⅔ innings. His 4.6 WAR was down from 6.7 and 6.4, respectively, in the previous two seasons, but he made five fewer starts. Normally, a pitcher like Skubal hitting free agency would mean bidding into the mid-nine-figure range, but there's uncertainty this time around with the CBA expiring and the ownership side driving hard toward a salary cap. It's possible that Skubal's contract needs to wait until after a deal is made between the two sides and teams know what they have to work with in their finances. Conversely, a team could be incredibly aggressive in trying to get his deal grandfathered under the previous CBA. Time will tell. 
For now, Skubal and the rest of the Dodgers head home for the winter.

title: Who's to blame for Dodgers' shocking NLCS loss vs. Brewers? Five places to point fingers - CBS Sports
description: The Dodgers were swept in the NLCS, and the blame can be shared by Freddie Freeman, Shohei Ohtani and others
body:
The Dodgers were swept in the NLCS, and the blame can be shared by Freddie Freeman, Shohei Ohtani and others
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:38 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Milwaukee Brewers are going to the World Series for the second time in franchise history and the first time as a National League team (the Brewers were still in the American League when they went to the World Series in 1982). This also means the Los Angeles Dodgers have been eliminated, and their shot at becoming baseball's first threepeat champion since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees ended on Thursday night. The Brewers have swept the Dodgers in four games in the NLCS, doing so one year after the Dodgers swept them in the 2025 NLCS.Who is to blame for the Dodgers going four-and-out in the NLCS? There's plenty of blame to go around, so let's assign it, shall we?
                            
    
                                                
                    
      1. The Brewers  Milwaukee continues to be baseball's best teamWe have to start here. The Dodgers got swept in the NLCS because the Brewers outplayed them in every phase of the game. The Brewers got better starting pitching. Their bullpen was better. Their defense and baserunning were better. Their offense was better at both stringing together hits to build a rally and launching the ball out of the park. Pat Murphy out-managed Dave Roberts as well. You name it, and the Brewers did it better than the Dodgers this series.  "It's a pretty simple answer," Dodgers infielder Max Muncy said after Game 3. "We're playing like shit. They're playing great."
As much as we want to (and will) blame various Dodgers for the sweep, the single biggest reason they got swept is that the Brewers were simply the better team. They were the better team in the regular season based on their records (103-59 vs. 100-62) and run differentials (+214 vs. +201), and they certainly played like the better team in the NLCS. The better team doesn't always win a postseason series. In the NLCS though, the better team has played like the better team, period.    2. Shohei Ohtani  MLB's brightest star was greatly dimmed ... even with Game 4 homer
The biggest star on baseball's most star-laden team was not himself the last two months of the season. Shohei Ohtani played through knee and biceps injuries and had been so unproductive than Roberts said there would at least be a "conversation" about sitting Ohtani in Game 3. That didn't come to pass, and hey, Ohtani went 1 for 2 with a walk and a hit-by-pitch in Game 3, and hit a home run in Game 4. The homer put the Dodgers up 4-0 on Thursday. The Dodgers didn't score again. The bottom line is Ohtani was a non-factor until it was too late. It's hard to win when your best player is this diminished.Whenever a team loses in the postseason, the best player gets a disproportionate amount of the blame, and that applies to Ohtani this series. He's clearly not healthy, yet he insists on remaining in the lineup, and he's had multiple chances in the first three games to swing things in his team's favor, but couldn't do it. When the best player underperforms, he wears most of the blame. It has been the way of the world since the dawn of team sports. 
  3. Freddie Freeman  Normally clutch, Freeman has been the worst player in the series
Freddie Freeman, not Ohtani, was the worst player in the NLCS by both win probability added and championship probability added. He went 1 for 14 in the series and the one hit came in the first inning of Game 1. Freeman went 0 for 13 after his first NLCS at-bat and that 0 for 13 includes:  Striking out after Mookie Betts worked a leadoff walk in the third inning of Game 1.Grounding into an inning-ending double play in the fifth inning of Game 1.Popping up to second on the first pitch to lead off the eighth inning of Game 1.Flying out with runners on first and second and no outs in the third inning of Game 2.Flying out with runners on first and second and one out in the third inning of Game 3.Grounding out with a runner on first and two outs in the fifth inning of Game 3.That's an awful lot of empty at-bats in clutch situations for one of the best clutch hitters of this generation. Freeman had as many double plays as total bases (one each) in the NLCS, and his only RBI came on a sacrifice fly. You won't beat a team as good as the Brewers with sac flies. You need bigger swings from your best players and Freeman didn't provide them.     4. The supporting cast  Only two Dodgers hitters had consistently strong at-bats in the NLCSMax Muncy went 2 for 12 with six strikeouts in the NLCS. Teoscar Hernández went 3 for 14. Andy Pages went 3 for 12. Tommy Edman went 1 for 7. Will Smith went 2 for 15 in the NLCS. Postseason legend Enrique Hernández went 0 for 8 with a ghasty strikeout in Game 3. The Dodgers had runners at second and third with one out in sixth, and Hernández took two pitches in the zone for strikes, then flailed at slider out of the zone. It was maybe the single worst at-bat of this NLCS.  
Freeman was terrible, Ohtani was terrible, and the thing that has so often set the Dodgers apart these last few years -- an elite supporting cast -- was terrible as well. Edman, Muncy, Smith, and the Hernándezes are a combined 11 for 58 (.189) in the four games. Betts (3 for 15 with three walks) and Kyle Tucker (4 for 12 with three walks) were the only Dodgers hitters who escaped scrutiny. They were their most productive hitters and consistently had strong at-bats. Everyone else? 😴😴😴      5. Dave Roberts  Roberts did not push the right buttonsThe manager can not swing the bat or throw the ball for his players, but he can put his team in the best position to succeed, and Roberts did not do that in the NLCS. Game 3, especially, was a managerial mess. Roberts burned the precocious Josue De Paula in the sixth inning when he sent him up to pinch-hit for Miguel Rojas with runners on second and third and one out, then immediately pinch-hit Enrique Hernández for De Paula when the Brewers brought in a lefty reliever.  De Paula is a rookie, I get that, but he has a track record of hitting lefties well in the minors. More accurately, he has a strong track record of making contact against lefties, which is what the Dodgers needed in that spot. A ball in play to get a run home. Instead, Roberts defaulted to the veteran Hernández, who struck out feebly. For all his career postseason success, Hernández went 1 for 14 this postseason, and a .190/.235/.317 hitter in his last 19 postseason games. Roberts never adjusted his priors.  
The NLCS was a flashback to pre-2024 Roberts, when he too often showed too much faith in his veterans and had an unfortunate knack for sticking with starters too long. In 2024 and 2025, it all worked out, and Roberts looked like a genius. Those same mistakes, the ones he got away with the last two years, reared their ugly heads. The NLCS sweep is on the players, first and foremost. Roberts didn't play his cards well either. He's made things worse.

body:
With Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith missing practice, Fantasy managers should monitor Eagles, Lamar Jackson and Rashee Rice
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026
                            
                    at
    9:05 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            6 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Coming into Week 6, we knew things were going to be rough. This is one of the toughest bye weeks of the season, with five of the top 20 players on Draft Day off. The injury situation isn't making things any easier. There is positive news around Caleb Williams' return and at least some hope of an A.J. Brown return. If either of them plays, they will be ranked as starters. Most of the news early in the week has not been good. Nowhere has the news been as bad as it has been in Philadelphia.Jalen Hurts out with superficial blood clot, Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith not practicingThe long-term prognosis is still very much in the air, but what we do know is that Hurts won't play Week 6 against the Carolina Panthers. In his place will be Tanner McKee, who will play behind a makeshift line, possibly without Barkley and Smith, who are both dealing with hamstring issues. The Eagles' implied total has fallen to 17.75, one of the lowest marks of the week. McKee has made two starts in his NFL career and thrown 88 career passes. Both of his starts were in Week 18, so it is hard to know what, if anything, to take from them. We mostly agree with the line movement, that this is a significant downgrade, and if you have the luxury, the safest move may be to avoid Eagles not named Dallas Goedert. He's still a top 10 tight end and should be the team's leading target earner. Dameon Pierce is the next man up if Barkley can't go, and he projects as a low-end RB2 only because the position is so thin this week. Dontayvion Wicks is the top Eagles receiver if Smith is out, but he is a boom-bust WR3 who may not have much boom potential. If you don't like your DST, the Panthers have suddenly emerged as a legitimate starting option.Quinshon Judkins not practicing, KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston both limited on ThursdayOf these three, Boston is the only one we are currently projecting to play in Week 6. He's a WR3 with top 12 upside but a profile that suggests volatility. Concepcion is trying to work his way through the concussion protocol. It is a positive sign he got a limited session in on Wednesday but we won't rank him until he's cleared to play. If he's active, view him as a flex with upside. Judkins was in a walking boot on Sunday, and his backup, Raheim Sanders, was placed on Injured Reserve earlier in the week. That leaves Jaleel McLaughlin and Audric Estime, who the team just signed. McLaughling would be a mediocre flex if Judkins is out. Judkins would be a high-end flex if he plays. One guy who could complicate matters is Dylan Sampson, who logged his first limited practice on Thursday. We don't expect him to play, but keep an eye on what he does Friday.TreVeyon Henderson logs back-to-back limited sessionsHenderson has a high ankle sprain, so we didn't think he had any chance to play. The fact that he practiced on Wednesday and Thursday suggests otherwise.Rhamondre Stevenson will be ranked as a top 18 back either way, but he is a borderline top 12 option if Henderson is out. Henderson hasn't been startable for most of the season and we won't want to start him if he plays through the ankle injury.
Lamar Jackson still not practicing, Ravens wide receivers in fluxWe are hoping for Jackson's return but are currently ranking Tyler Huntley as the starter. Watch Friday's injury report, because if Jackson plays, we're obviously starting him. Ja'Kobi Lane is trying to get back from his IR stint and practiced in full on Wednesday and Thursday. We don't have him ranked yet, but would love to see him back. Rashod Bateman was a limited participant on Wednesday and then did not practice on Thursday. Neither of these guys will be ranked as more than a desperation flex if they play, but Lane may be someone worth stashing in deeper leagues. Zay Flowers was also listed as limited on Thursday, but he is expected to play.Tyjae Spears sits on ThursdaySpears was a limited participant on Wednesday, then sat out Thursday with a knee issue. The Titans have a good matchup against the Colts and Tony Pollard would be much easier to stomach as a starter if Spears wasn't cutting into his work. Either way, Pollard is an RB2, but he has real upside if Spears is out. If Spears plays, view him as a low-end PPR flex.Rico Dowdle logs full practice on ThursdayWe are moving Dowdle into our rankings on Thursday afternoon. This was close to an even split the first two weeks of the season but the Steelers have acknowledged that Jaylen Warren has been way too good to go back to an even timeshare. I am projecting 17 touches for Warren and 9 for Dowdle. That means Warren is still a top 12 running back while Dowdle is a decent flex. 
Rashee Rice not practicing again on ThursdayRice suffered a hamstring injury in Week 4 and it appears the bye week was not enough to get him back to 100%. The Chiefs are already without Tyquan Thornton, so Patrick Mahomes could need Jalen Royals and Cyrus Allen to play a major role against the Chargers. We aren't ruling Rice out yet, and rank him as a high-end WR3 due to injury risk. If Rice is out, Xavier Worthy would be a borderline WR2 and both Royals and Allen would have deep flex appeal. Mahomes could fall outside of our top 12 if Rice is out, and Kirk Cousins may be a better start.Kyle Monangai also out on ThursdayIt looks like it will be another week of D'Andre Swift and Roschon Johnson at running back for the Bears. Swift is an RB1 that should be started in all leagues, while Johnson is more of a low-end flex. They rotated drives last week, but Johnson was extremely inefficient as a rusher. If Monangai returns on Friday, he could be a high-end flex in Week 6.Jacory Croskey-Merrit not practicing ThursdayThis was the first practice of the week for the Commanders, who play San Francisco on Monday. This backfield is a mess right now with Croskey-Merritt, Rachaad White, and Austin Ekeler all getting touches. I don't really want to start any of them, especially against a good defense like the 49ers. That being said, Croskey-Merritt is our favorite if he plays. If he's out, then Rachaad White becomes much more appealing as a high-end flex, especially in PPR.
Almost all of the Chargers' receivers appear to be questionableLadd McConkey, Quentin Johnston, KeAndre Lambert-Smith, Marquez Valdes-Scantling, and Brenen Thompson were all limited on Thursday. The only notable name who wasn't questionable is Tre Harris, who is out for multiple weeks. Even if all these guys return, we wouldn't want to start Justin Herbert against the Chiefs with the current state of his offensive line. The one guy who could become a Fantasy starter this week is Ladd McConket, but I would like to see a full practice first.Jeremiyah Love still not practicingLove missed practice on Wednesday and Thursday. He has an ankle injury, but he also sounds like he's really run-down. The Cardinals may choose to give him a week to heal up, but he hasn't been ruled out yet. If Love is out, then Tyler Allgeier is a high-end flex, right about where Love is ranked between RB25 and RB30. This is a bad matchup and the Cardinals will probably be chasing the score.David Montgomery not traveling to LondonWoody Marks will be the lead back for the Texans in an uneven matchup. The Jaguars are arguably the best run defense in football, but they are also giving up six catches per week to opposing running backs. It's a statement on the position this week that Marks is a top-20 back because we are very concerned about his rushing efficiency, but he should catch enough passes to be startable in PPR.

title: Cowboys QB Dak Prescott urges players to speak up after Jalen Hurts diagnosis - CBS Sports
description: The Cowboys quarterback called Hurts' condition "scary" and encouraged athletes to communicate openly with medica
body:
The Cowboys quarterback called Hurts' condition "scary" and encouraged athletes to communicate openly with medical personnel
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026
                            
                    at
    7:13 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        FRISCO, Texas -- News of Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts being ruled out in Week 6 with a superficial blood clot shook many NFL players, including rival Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott."It's scary when you get things like that. Blood clots, you're talking about someone's life, especially with the plane trip and all that they took," Prescott said. "Yeah, it's scary. If you're feeling something, speak up on it. I'm fortunate I have [my personal physical therapist] Luke Miller. He's on things before I'm on things at times. I try to blow things off, and he's like 'no, no let's look at this. Let me get a better check on it.' I encourage people to be open about their body and learn about their body." In a statement about the injury, the Eagles said Hurts visited the training room on Thursday, Oct. 8, after practice to receive treatment on his calf. Philadelphia had an ultrasound of his calf done on Saturday after the team flew to London for their Week 5 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars, and it picked up a superficial blood clot. In tandem with London doctors, the team's medical staff decided Hurts could play safely. After a follow-up ultrasound, it was discovered Hurts' blood clot had moved, so the Eagles ruled him out for their Week 6 game against the Carolina Panthers, saying "his health and safety are our highest priority." Prescott's message to other athletes in light of this situation is straightforward: have open conversations with your team's training staff. He acknowledged there can sometimes be a stigma to doing so as an NFL player, but there's nothing wrong with putting things on their radar. 
"I'm in a fortunate situation now being this far into my career, but it's about making good relationships with those guys [the training staff]," Prescott said. "Tell them everything. You can get a heads up on it. You can tell them and just say 'it's fine, but I'm letting you know.' I encourage all athletes: don't be shy if something is bothering you. Speak up on it. This is a tough man's sport at the end of the day, so let them know if you're fine like 'hey, I'm just warning you. I'm just alerting you, so you can get ahead of things like this.'"

        In the Week 6 edition of "Thursday Night Football," the Denver Broncos play host to the Seattle Seahawks.The Broncos are coming off their third win in the last four games, though it required a late, game-winning drive against the decrepit division rival Los Angeles Chargers. The return of Sean Payton as play-caller didn't exactly result in an explosive or efficient offense, but the Broncos did just enough to hold off L.A. and climb back over .500.The Seahawks, meanwhile, dropped to 3-2 after falling to their own division rivals in the San Francisco 49ers. The Niners moved the ball quite well against the vaunted Seattle defense, and turnovers in their own territory haunted the Seahawks and ultimately cost them the game.Will the Seahawks bounce back, or will the Broncos capture their second consecutive victory? We'll find out soon enough. Before we break down the matchup, here's a look at how you can watch the game.
Where to watch Broncos vs. Seahawks liveDate: Thursday, Oct. 15 | Time: 8:20 p.m. ETLocation: Empower Field at Mile High (Denver)Streaming: Amazon PrimeFollow: CBS Sports AppOdds: Seahawks -2.5, O/U 40.5 via DraftKings SportsbookWhen the Seahawks have the ballLet's start here: the Seahawks cannot run the ball at all. They couldn't run the ball when rookie running back Jadarian Price was healthy earlier in the season, and they haven't been able to run the ball since he's been out. The trio of Price, Emanuel Wilson and George Holani has combined for just 447 yards on 127 carries -- an average of just 3.5 per tote. The Seahawks do not get much push up front, as their backs average a mere 0.69 yards before contact per carry, a figure that ranks fourth-worst in the NFL, according to Tru Media. Their 2.83 yards after contact per carry is more respectable, ranking 14th league-wide.The Broncos will have to be careful there. They've allowed the third-fewest rushing yards before contact per carry in the league so far (0.59), but the most rushing yards after contact (3.92), thanks to a sky-high avoided tackle rate by enemy backs (30.1%). Much of that production came from Kenneth Walker III in the season opener, but even in Weeks 2 through 5, the Broncos rank in the bottom third of the league in both yards after contact per attempt and broken tackle rate.
Wilson is likely to be the primary runner once again while Price and Zach Charbonnet remain sidelined. The Broncos will have to get him on the ground on the first try, limiting the yards he can gain after contact, because the Seahawks just don't create much for him in the first place. He scarcely gets more than is blocked without breaking through tackles.In the passing game, Sam Darnold has struggled to replicate last year's results -- especially over the last two weeks. In games against the Chargers and 49ers, Darnold went just 31-of-51 for 363 yards, three touchdowns and three interceptions. After leading the league in turnovers last season, Darnold has already been picked off five times in his three full appearances this season, while his yards per attempt average is down from 8.5 to just 7.7. His completion rate is down over 3 percentage points as well.Denver's pass defense has been largely good so far this year, with the Broncos ranking fifth in opponents' EPA per dropback, according to Tru Media. The Broncos just held the Chargers to 82 net passing yards last week, which plays a huge role in that figure, but they've also allowed only one team (Rams) to top 218 net passing yards in any game so far. (The Chiefs didn't have to throw the ball very much in Week 1, though, because they did whatever they wanted on the ground.)
The Broncos won't have Patrick Surtain II or Talanoa Hufanga here, and Riley Moss is listed as questionable -- all of which is a significant issue when you're going up against Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who leads the NFL in both receiving yards and receiving touchdowns. Jahdae Barron and Kris Abrams-Draine figure to see increased roles due to the cornerback injuries, while Devon Key will play more in the wake of Hufanga's absence. They'll all have their work cut out for them against JSN. The Seahawks really don't throw the ball to anyone else all that often.When the Broncos have the ballDenver might have gotten a win last week, but Sean Payton's return as play-caller didn't have much to do with it. The Broncos entered the game against the Chargers averaging a miserable 4.9 yards per play, then averaged a mere 3.9 per play in the win over Los Angeles. Bo Nix totaled just 123 yards on his 27 pass attempts, J.K. Dobbins ran for only 68 yards on his 18 carries, Jaylen Waddle caught just two of five balls thrown his way for just 19 yards ... nothing went well offensively. And nothing has gone right pretty much all year, with the exception of the second halves of the Broncos' wins over the Jaguars and Rams in Weeks 2 and 3. Two good halves in five weeks isn't much to write home about, even if those halves helped the Broncos steal a pair of wins and arrive at 3-2.
Nix is essentially refusing to push the ball down the field so far this season. His average air yards per attempt in each of his first two years of his career was 7.3, according to Tru Media, but that figure has dropped all the way to 5.2 this year. He threw deep on 13.1% of his passes as a rookie and 11.8% of them last year, but he's done so on only 7.4% of his attempts this season. Nix also isn't running anymore. He scrambled 27.3% of the time when pressured during his rookie season and 16.1% of the time last season. That number is all the way down to 5.6% so far this year, meaning he's scrambled only four times in five games. All of this, combined with his insistence on checking down repeatedly, has made the pass offense feel neutered to date.Meanwhile, the Broncos also can't run the ball. Dobbins looks like he's running with a piano on his back, slogging his way to 3.6 yards per carry. RJ Harvey barely gets opportunities, but he hasn't done any better at only 3.7 yards per carry. Harvey is at least productive in the short passing game, but the Broncos de-emphasized that last week under Payton in favor of more Dobbins runs that went nowhere.
The Seahawks have largely been their usual selves defensively through the first five weeks of the season. They've arrived at their two losses largely by virtue of their offense repeatedly turning the ball over against the Commanders (three times) and 49ers (four, including a fumble that resulted in a touchdown). Seattle has held opponents to the fewest passing yards in the league and the fewest net yards per attempt, and it has limited running games to the eighth-fewest yards per attempt as well. It's hard to see the Broncos snapping out of their funk against this unit.PredictionSean Payton's return to calling plays may have let the Broncos come away with a win, but it did not result in their offense looking competent. They averaged just 3.9 yards per play against what had previously been a very bad Chargers defense. I cannot rightly expect the Broncos to get anything going against this hellacious Seattle defense. It's not like the Broncos are going to do what the 49ers did. Denver is also still banged up defensively and likely won't have Surtain here, which is obviously a problem against JSN.  Pick: Seahawks 24, Broncos 16

title: Broncos' cheating accusation against Seahawks almost led to lawsuit in 2024, according to Mike Macdonald - CBS Sports
description: This is one of the wildest stories you'll ever hear in the NFL

This is one of the wildest stories you'll ever hear in the NFL

        Last season almost ended with the Denver Broncos facing the Seattle Seahawks in the Super Bowl, and if that game would have happened, there likely would have been some serious drama, because it seems the two head coaches don't like each other very much. Just ask Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald about that. "He's not my biggest fan," Macdonald recently said of Broncos' coach Sean Payton. During a recent interview with Graham Bensinger, Macdonald spilled the details on a wild story from 2024 involving Payton. In his first game ever as a head coach, Macdonald led his team to a 26-20 road win over the Broncos to open the 2024 season. During the game, the Seahawks' defense seemed to always be one step ahead of Denver's offense: They forced three turnovers while holding the Broncos to just 231 yards. 
Since it was Week 1, Macdonald didn't have a lot of film on the Broncos, so he decided to turn to Twitter to see if he could find some plays they might use. "Fans will tape and post plays from training camp on Twitter, so it's public knowledge, so we took like a 100 plays from their training camp," Macdonald said. "We're scouting them."At some point after the game was played, Payton somehow found out about the Seahawks' social media scouting session and he was NOT happy. 
"He got wind of it and he lost it," Macdonald said. Broncos threatened to go to the NFLPayton was so upset with what Seattle did that he threated to turn them into the NFL. It got so serious that Payton actually reached out to Seahawks general manger John Schneider. "So he called John and he basically threatened to come out publicly and do a whole Patriot, like Spygate type of thing," Macdonald said. "And I'm sitting there like, 'Oh my God, we didn't cheat.' He thought it was a Michigan thing where we had a plant."So it appears that Payton thought the Seahawks may have actually sent someone to Broncos' training camp, which would be illegal, but Macdonald says all the plays came from Twitter, which wouldn't violate any NFL rules. The Seahawks were so sure that they didn't break any rules that they threatened to SUE Payton if he reached out to the league. 
"So we had to counter with him, to say like, 'Hey, look, if you come out at us, we're going to sue you, because it's not true,'" Macdonald said. "So he backed down, but he was killing John, our GM."None of this ever leaked out and the reason for that is because Payton eventually put it behind him. "So the season ends and he let it go," Macdonald said. Fallout for the BroncosPayton might have let it go, but the Seahawks' strategy appears to have led to a major change at Broncos training camp. It is now prohibited for fans to take video at any of Denver's training camp practices. During their 2026 camp, the Broncos posted signs all around the facility so that fans knew they could be kicked out if they were excessively breaking the rules. 
Allowing fans and media to film plays at training camp has become a touchy issue around the NFL. Some teams permit it, but most of them are like the Broncos and have rules against it. Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley was in a similar situation last season when he was the defensive coordinator for the Packers. At the time, Kevin Patullo, who is now a Dolphins assistant, was the Eagles offensive coordinator and Philadelphia scouted the Packers by using a training camp play they spotted on social media. "We had a pressure I had never run, so there's no way he could've known about it," Hafley said earlier this month. "And they knew it was coming. (Kevin) said they saw it on video."
With the Payton-Macdonald feud now going public, teams may decide to revisit their social media policies when it comes to fans at training camp. For Macdonald, scouting plays on Twitter ended up working out, which isn't a huge surprise, because most things seem to end up working out for him. The Seahawks head coach won a Lombardi Trophy last season in just his second year on the job. The Seahawks beat the Patriots in Super Bowl LX and they came close to facing the Broncos: Denver came up just one game short of getting to the Super Bowl with a loss in the AFC title game.

        Following consecutive practices of full participation, Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams is on track for a potential return in Week 6 from the hamstring injury he sustained in the second game of the season. It remains to be seen whether he will enter Sunday's matchup against the Atlanta Falcons with an injury designation, but he said on Thursday that he still does not know if he will play.While the understanding outside the Bears' facility is that Williams sustained a Grade 2 hamstring strain in the Week 2 loss to the Minnesota Vikings, the third-year quarterback pushed back against reports detailing the extent of the injury. He said he felt a pop in his hamstring at the time of the injury and described it as a tear rather than a strain."It was a hamstring tear and a pretty serious one," Williams said. "We got a grade, but I wouldn't say it's deserved to be put out there after all the false ones. So next question."Williams repeatedly declined to detail the official diagnosis."There's nothing that has come out that has been right about what it is and what it has been," Williams said. "That's been fun to deal with. So I would say from y'all's side and things like that is being able to report it and go through it in the right way and right manner. And then from there, if you haven't heard it from boss man himself or out of the horse's mouth, me, it would probably be wrong, which every single one has been."
Coach Ben Johnson initially labeled Williams as week-to-week after the team received the results of his MRI. Tyson Bagent and Case Keenum split the quarterback duties over the last three games.Caleb Williams pushes back on injury narrativesNot only did Williams take exception to the reporting on his hamstring injury, but he also noticed the discourse surrounding his on-field demeanor. Williams was in clear distress in the immediate wake of the injury as he yelled in agony and was emotional when he left the field on a cart. He had a towel over his head as he was transported to the locker room and shed tears while giving a thumbs-up to the Chicago crowd.
When initial reports and the Bears' handling of the injury suggested that it may not be as serious as feared, fans were quick to judge Williams for what some called an overreaction.
"I'm always gonna show emotion, especially when I can't be out there with the guys when something like that happens," Williams said. "I care about the team, the organization, winning, being out there, my teammates, all of that. I care. That's the biggest thing. This is what I love to do. This puts a smile on my face. It's everything to me."Not being able to be out there was frustrating. That was more of the tears or whatever that was. The other half of it was just everybody making jokes and all of that. But that doesn't bother me. It's the other half of the national or the local [media] and them putting out false things that weren't true to then allow people to go run with it."Dating back to his college career at USC, Williams continues to be the subject of scrutiny for his perceived toughness. The response to his hamstring injury is the latest example, as fans also called into question his nail-painting, the emotions he shed after a tough loss to rival UCLA, and more.
"My character's been attacked for a while," Williams said. "It's just another motivating factor when I get out there and get going again."

title: Who is Tanner McKee? Eagles QB's college, NFL career and path to replacing Jalen Hurts - CBS Sports
description: The former Stanford quarterback takes over for Jalen Hurts with Philadelphia trying to end a three-game skid and
body:
The former Stanford quarterback takes over for Jalen Hurts with Philadelphia trying to end a three-game skid and remain in the NFC East race
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:32 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            7 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The task of breaking a three-game losing streak and keeping the Philadelphia Eagles afloat in the NFC East falls not on Jalen Hurts in Week 6 but rather on Tanner McKee, a fourth-year backup primed for the biggest opportunity of his NFL career. Hurts is out for the matchup against the Carolina Panthers due to a superficial blood clot, which developed after the Week 4 loss to the Los Angeles Rams and moved following last week's trip to London, resulting in his unavailability for Sunday.While the Eagles do have a third option in rookie Cole Payton, the expectation is that McKee will trot out with the offense when they return to Lincoln Financial Field. He served as Hurts' primary backup last year and was the third-stringer in 2024 and made a combined six appearances with two starts.McKee is not entirely unknown in the NFL, considering his pair of previous starts, but this is by far the most prominent role of his career. With so much pressure facing the Eagles in their quest to rebound from a rocky start to the season, McKee will have more eyes on him this weekend than ever before.So who is McKee, really? Here is everything to know about his football career, from his rise as a highly touted high school recruit to his emergence as Philadelphia's Week 6 starter.
Blue-chip recruitMcKee landed on the national radar during his junior year at Corona (Calif.) High School. Centennial. It was the most productive season of his prep career and earned him recognition as a Top247 recruit, and he later climbed as high as No. 38 overall in the 247Sports rankings for the Class of 2018. McKee closed the recruiting cycle as the top four-star quarterback with only three five-star prospects ahead of him: Trevor Lawrence, Justin Fields and JT Daniels.
As a three-sport athlete who also played volleyball and basketball at Centennial, McKee's future was always in football, and he elevated his stock with strong showings on the all-star circuit. He won the MVP award at the 2018 Polynesian Bowl, earned a spot in the U.S. Army All-American Bowl and reached the finals at both The Opening and Elite 11.McKee already held scholarship offers from myriad Power Five schools when Stanford called. Programs across the country sought his talents. Even though Stanford was his ultimate choice and much closer to home than the other programs he was interested in, it was not an open-and-shut case that he would end up with the Cardinal. Stanford was the last school to extend him an offer and the penultimate school to welcome him for an official visit. By the time he took his official visit in January 2018, he had already been on campus for regular-season games at Texas, Texas A&M, Alabama and Washington.
Each of those other schools pushed hard to land him, but come National Signing Day in February 2018, it was Stanford that earned McKee's commitment. The only hiccup for the Cardinal was that its prized signee would not arrive for another two years.The long road to Stanford's lineupAs a member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, McKee embarked on a two-year mission in Brazil. The COVID-19 pandemic cut his mission short by about five weeks, and upon his return to the United States, uncertainty about the 2020 college football season left him without a firm answer as to when he would join the Cardinal and eventually suit up as a freshman quarterback. His roster spot was waiting for him, though, and he was physically ready to join the team thanks to a workout regimen he and a fellow missionary adhered to in Brazil."Because we had that weight room in my last area, I think I gained back 10 pounds," McKee said to Deseret News after returning from his mission. "That was super nice. We worked out every morning and I was able to get a little bit back in shape. He threw the rugby ball and I threw the football. Now, when I throw, my arm doesn't really get sore. It's nice to come back home and work out at full speed."
The Pac-12 delayed the start of its season due to the pandemic and was the last of the power conferences to begin play. Stanford held just six games that year, with one against Washington State canceled due to virus protocols. McKee was supposed to be the No. 3 quarterback on Stanford's roster but was elevated to the backup job in the opener when a false positive COVID-19 test kept Davis Mills out of action. That game against No. 12 Oregon got out of hand, and McKee made his lone appearance of the season late in a 35-14 loss.Mills departed for the NFL at the end of that campaign, which sparked a competition between McKee and incumbent backup Jack West for the starting job in 2021. West won the job out of fall camp but lost it when he threw two interceptions in a 24-7 season-opening loss to Kansas State. McKee took over and never looked back.Emergence as NFL prospectThe first start of McKee's college career was an indication of the highlights to come. He orchestrated a 42-28 upset win on the road at No. 14 USC and kept the momentum rolling with two more wins in the next three games, including one over the same Oregon team that defeated the Cardinal the year prior. The Ducks were the No. 3 team in the nation at the time and stood on the wrong end of a breakout performance for McKee in which he racked up 230 yards and three touchdowns in an overtime thriller.
That Oct. 2 victory was the last of Stanford's season, though, as everything went off the rails. McKee missed two games due to injury during a seven-game losing streak to close the year.While the team's overall struggles continued into a three-win 20222 season, McKee did his part as one of the few bright spots on the roster. He started all 12 games and posted a 62% completion rate with 2,947 passing yards and 13 touchdowns to eight interceptions. He also ran for two scores.McKee's performance as a two-year starter made him a draftable quarterback and led him to leave Stanford a year early. He declared for the 2023 NFL Draft and was selected with the 188th overall pick in the sixth round. That marked the start of what is now a four-year tenure with the Eagles.
Career backup with a Super Bowl ringHurts had already established himself as a star quarterback by the time McKee arrived in Philadelphia. He was fresh off the best year of his career: A 2022 campaign in which he earned second-team All-Pro recognition. McKee was never going to be more than a backup, and he spent his rookie year in the No. 3 role behind Hurts and Marcus Mariota. He did not play that season.McKee's first opportunity for playing time came in 2024. With Hurts in concussion protocol and backup Kenny Pickett dealing with an in-game rib injury, McKee was thrust into action in Week 17, and he could not have performed much better as two of his three completions went for touchdowns.
McKee then made his first career start in the regular-season finale and was similarly effective in a 27-for-41, 269-yard, two-touchdown win over the New York Giants. The best part of that season, though? McKee was on the sideline when the Eagles won the Super Bowl.
It was not until Week 18 of the following season that McKee returned to the starting lineup. The Eagles had already locked up their postseason position and rested their starters, and with McKee holding the primary backup job that year, he was the next man up at quarterback. He threw for 241 yards and a touchdown but also logged his first career interception in a loss to the Washington Commanders.First meaningful startWhen McKee leads the Philadelphia offense onto the field on Sunday, it will be his first start outside of Week 18. And depending on the severity of Hurts' blood clot and how long it takes for him to return to the lineup, McKee might be in line to make consecutive starts for the first time. Once Hurts is cleared to play, though, the Eagles will almost certainly thrust him back into action. Even amid a difficult start to the year and even as it seems the Eagles could be trending toward a rebuild, everything is still ahead of them.McKee will have a chance to solidify his job as a No. 2 NFL quarterback against the Panthers, but the chances of a strong performance amounting to much more than that are slim. This is a prime spot for him to shine, considering the Panthers' defense is undermanned and just allowed 32 points in its last outing. Starting cornerbacks Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson are on injured reserve, which opens the door for McKee to pick apart the back end of the Carolina defense. He might have to do it without top wide receiver DeVonta Smith, though, as he continues to nurse a hamstring injury.

title: Jayden Daniels takes blame for Commanders' embarrassing gaffe vs. Giants: 'Will never happen again' - CBS Sports

Daniels defended Dan Quinn on Thursday and shouldered full responsibility for Washington letting the clock run out in field goal range
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026

    4:31 pm ET

            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Washington Commanders had what will likely go down as the most embarrassing moment of the 2026 NFL season, as they ran the clock out on themselves in field goal range in overtime vs. the New York Giants, leading to a 27-27 tie.Following a wild game that led directly into a bonkers overtime, the Commanders took over possession at their own 23-yard line with 1:55 remaining in overtime and zero timeouts. A 16-yard gain from Terry McLaurin, followed by a Jayden Daniels scramble of 16 yards and a Treylon Burks reception of 13 yards, got Washington into field goal territory with 55 seconds remaining.On what ended up being the final play of the game, Daniels took a dive at the Giants' 24-yard line with eight seconds remaining on the clock. His offense couldn't get back to the line of scrimmage to spike the ball before it hit triple zeros. 
There's a lot of blame to go around for this catastrophe, including head coach Dan Quinn. However, in speaking to reporters on Thursday, Daniels made sure to declare himself the main reason Washington left Week 5 with a tie rather than a win. 
"Ultimately, it's on me at the end of the day," Daniels told reporters. "I know DQ is getting a lot of slack for it or whatever, but regardless of what happens, I'm the person on the field that's supposed to calm everything, control everything and I failed to the standard that I hold myself to and the standard in this organization. "This is something for me to move on, not saying I'm proud of it or anything. Obviously, looking back, it could have resulted in a loss. We tied, but it was a failure in my eyes, and I know I'm better than that. I hold myself to a higher standard than that. So moving forward, I'll grow from it, learn from it, and it'll never happen again." Daniels isn't wrong. Whether your head coach is Bill Belichick or a first-year guy, the quarterback is responsible for the operation of the offense. Daniels saw the running clock at 13 seconds when he snapped the ball on that final play. At that point, you're throwing it away to the sideline or throwing it in the dirt. You're not taking a sack or going down inbounds. No starting quarterback should have to be told that. 
While Quinn has taken much of the blame from the media after the gaffe, Daniels hasn't been without criticism, too. Packers' edge rusher Micah Parsons ripped into the quarterback on his podcast, saying he "probably cost Dan Quinn his job.""All respectfully, we get coached so much on these situations that, like, I'm a defensive player, and this shit's programmed to me," Parsons said. "I even know what to do in those situations. There's no way I'm taking a sack with 14 seconds left and no timeouts...And, mind you, it'd be different if Jayden Daniels was a rookie. This is your third year. This is your third year. You've been to the NFC Championship game. You've been in big moments before. And to me, like even after a sack, you're casually getting up. ... He's not even urgently getting up. ... That is disgusting, bro."It was a bizarre sequence. Why did the Commanders' players on the field not show any urgency to get back to the line of scrimmage when Daniels went down? Why did David Blough call for a play with motion as the clock continued to tick? What was Daniels trying to do on that final play? The football world may never know.

        Jeff Lebby knows Lane Kiffin better than most. Lebby ran Kiffin's offense at Ole Miss in 2020 and 2021, and the Rebels' 2020 attack set an SEC record for total offense in conference play. Kiffin called him "a huge part of our success there" this week. Now Mississippi State's head coach, he leads the Bulldogs into a top-25 showdown with LSU on Saturday."I don't like playing against him because they go so fast," Kiffin said this week.LSU (4-2, 1-2 SEC) is reeling after an overtime loss at Kentucky last week, and finds itself in a familiar place under previous coaches: two losses at the midpoint of the season. It wasn't supposed to start this way for Kiffin, who took over a program with deep pockets and turned the roster over into one of the most talented in the country. A third conference loss in Kiffin's first season would leave almost no margin for November, with Alabama and Texas still coming to Baton Rouge.
Mississippi State (4-1, 2-1) has already won two SEC games, exceeding the one Lebby collected in his first two seasons combined. Alabama rode into Starkville and won 56-23 two weeks ago, and Kamario Taylor, the sophomore quarterback who spent September in the Heisman Trophy conversation, finished the day on the sideline with a boot on his right foot.Two weeks later, nobody outside the Bulldogs' building knows if he will play. Lebby said the SEC availability report would answer that question. LSU vs. Mississippi State: Need to knowKamario Taylor's right foot: Taylor has thrown for 1,450 yards and an SEC-best 17 touchdowns with four interceptions. He's thrown three touchdowns in the last five games, the longest stretch since LSU's Jayden Daniels in 2023. He first hurt his foot in the win over Missouri, and it showed against the Tide. He was sacked five times and finished with minus-26 rushing yards before leaving the game. If he can't play, Lebby's options are redshirt freshman Parker Puckett and AJ Swann, who spent a season at LSU. 
Where is Mississippi State's ground game? Fluff Bothwell has 403 yards and three touchdowns on 74 carries, but he had only one carry against Alabama and spent most of the afternoon with a boot on his left foot. The Bulldogs were outrushed 179-18. Now they get a defense that ranked second nationally against the run through four weeks, allowing 47.5 yards per game. Kentucky found cracks last week. The Wildcats ran for 155 yards.The Sam Leavitt Experience: LSU QB Sam Leavitt has thrown for 1,496 yards and 10 touchdowns, but he has thrown an interception in every game this season, totaling eight through six games. At Kentucky, he completed 25 of 34 passes for 275 yards and two touchdowns and ran for another in overtime, but he also threw a pick and lost a fumble on a sack in the fourth quarter. LSU's recent success: The Tigers have won the last three meetings against Mississippi State. The Bulldogs last won in Baton Rouge in 2020, when they pulled off a 44-34 upset in Mike Leach's first season. This is the first meeting since 2023. The teams used to play each other annually, but that ended when the SEC expanded to 16 teams in 2024.

title: Is the Dodgers' dynasty over? Three reasons why Los Angeles' dominance could be nearing an end - CBS Sports
description: The Dodgers' aging core of superstars struggled mightily in a four-game NLCS sweep at the hands of the Brewers
body:
The Dodgers' aging core of superstars struggled mightily in a four-game NLCS sweep at the hands of the Brewers
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:09 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            7 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        First, yes, the premise is true: The Los Angeles Dodgers are every bit a modern baseball dynasty. They've won three of the last six World Series. They've won 13 of the last 14 National League West titles and they've made the playoffs for 14 straight years. Over the last decade, they've amassed six 100-win seasons, and that total almost certainly would be seven if 2020 had been a standard 162-game campaign (their 43-17 record that year was a 116-win pace). The Dodgers across those last 10 seasons have outscored their opponents by a cumulative total of 2,102 runs, which is frankly ridiculous. In second place are the Houston Astros with a run differential of +1,376 since the start of the 2017 season. There's topping all comers, and then there's overwhelming them. This is the latter. So, yes, the Dodgers are a dynasty.Now, though, that dynasty is in peril. The Milwaukee Brewers swept the Dodgers in four games in the National League Championship Series, ending Los Angeles' hunt for the elusive World Series three-peat. Neither will they win the World Series for the 10th time in franchise history, at least not this year. On Thursday, the Dodgers suffered their first loss in an elimination contest since Game 3 of the 2023 NLDS. This time, however, feels different, more substantial and with greater forward-looking implications for baseball's flagship franchise. 
Because of that, it's time to ponder whether the Dodgers' dynasty is in its waning days. It's impossible to say for certain, of course, but there are three general reasons the Dodgers' current run of dominance may – may! – be coming to an end. Let's explore those reasons now. 1. The Dodgers are getting oldThe Dodgers this season had the oldest crop of position players in all of MLB, with an average age of 30.9 years. Moreover, a number of core contributors are reaching the age at which deep decline becomes a real possibility. In 2027, Freddie Freeman will be in his age-37 campaign. Max Muncy will be in his age-36 season. Mookie Betts recently turned 34. Teoscar Hernández turned 34 on Thursday. Will Smith turns 32 in March, and we know all about the accelerated aging curves of catchers. Shohei Ohtani is only 32 -- not necessarily a concerning age for a future Hall of Famer -- but no one has been worked harder and has more wear, tear, and fatigue layered upon him over the past several years than the two-way superstar. This is just the eventual cost of doing business when you build aggressively through free agency and trades paired with long-term extensions as the Dodgers have. To be sure, it's been worth it beyond anyone's hopes, but eventually the bill comes due in the form of high-salary stars on the downsides of their careers. 

        
            
                Who's to blame for Dodgers' shocking NLCS loss vs. Brewers? Five places to point fingers
                
                    Mike Axisa                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
On the pitching front, they're not quite as long in the tooth, but of the established starting pitchers, only Yoshinobu Yamamoto will be on the right side of age 30 next season. That same rotation is shot through with persistent injury concerns, and the Dodgers, for all their organizational merits, aren't famous for keeping pitchers healthy. There's also no guarantee that they'll be able to retain the services of trade deadline acquisition Tarik Skubal this coming offseason. To be sure, all is not bleak, as the Dodgers have a strong farm system and an impressive base of young talent. Andy Pages and Dalton Rushing to some extent, but most especially Josue De Paula figures to lift both floor and ceiling, and there's more on the way. However, those in-place and incoming young players may indeed have a hard time replicating the past dynastic excellence of the Dodgers' current core, and it may be some time before they're even ready to try. Not all of them, of course, will work out. In the meantime, the Dodgers must hope that decline isn't linear for those veteran names above. That's especially key since the upcoming free-agent class will provide starkly little frontline help beyond Skubal.  2. The next CBA will directly target themNegotiations are ongoing for the next Collective Bargaining Agreement, and whatever comes out of that complicated wash will very likely affect the Dodgers and their spending capacity in a major way. 
The MLBPA -- the union representing the players in these talks -- will probably never agree to a cap-and-floor system that team owners are demanding, but such an outcome is at least possible. The entire rhetorical push for a cap from the league side is centered on the Dodgers, and whatever structural changes emerge will target the top-end spenders. Speaking of which, there's already meaningful common ground between players and owners when it comes to making sweeping changes to how MLB shares local revenues, especially local broadcast revenues.Commissioner Rob Manfred and the owners who tell him what to do want to bundle all these various and sundry local broadcast rights as one, similar to what the NFL does, and peddle them to the highest bidder (or bidders) once the national broadcast rights are up for renegotiation in 2028. With regard to the Dodgers, this writer recently went a-writin' about this very matter. Here's the relevant excerpt:This is keenly relevant to the Dodgers. Under former owner/saboteur Frank McCourt, the Dodgers were in bankruptcy proceedings when McCourt sold them to the current owners, the Guggenheim Group. As a consequence of those court proceedings and a resulting settlement with the league, the Dodgers, after signing an $8.35 billion deal with Time-Warner, were obligated to share a much smaller percentage of their local broadcast revenues than other teams were. The Dodgers on average take in $334 million per year in local broadcast revenues, and that figure grows a bit each year since the contract is backloaded (by the end of it, their annual take will be more than $500 million). By contrast, the Marlins in recent years made less than $50 million each year in local broadcast monies, and even the flagship Yankees take in less than half of what the Dodgers do on an average annual basis, at least in terms of local broadcast revenues. Call it the "Dodgers Exception" if you like. It's not only giving the Dodgers much greater financial latitude, but it's also keeping money out of the revenue-sharing pool. That Dodgers broadcast contract runs through 2038, by the way, with a higher payout each year.…Nationalizing such broadcasts would eliminate that competitive advantage because it would require MLB to buy out the Dodgers' contract and or purchase the Dodgers' regional sports network.While the MLBPA is not yet on board with such a drastic overhaul of the current revenue-sharing system -- they want some incentives to remain for small-market owners to actually invest in the product, which most of them barely do -- there is some meaningful shared territory here. Indeed, in their opening proposal to the league back in May, the union called for steeply increased sharing of local broadcast revenues. The upshot is that the next CBA will involve a significant transfer of revenues from large-market clubs to small-market clubs on a sustained basis. That means a financial haircut for the Dodgers and less room in the budget to do what they've been doing so well for the past decade or so.Whatever the specifics, it's a near certainty that the new CBA, which will take effect before the 2027 season begins -- whenever that is -- will make the Dodgers' "dynasty maintenance program" far more difficult. 3. The ownership situation is troubled and perhaps uncertainNo, this isn't as dire as Frank McCourt somehow managing to bankrupt the cash-printing Dodgers, but principal owner Mark Walter has serious legal and financial worries right now. Once the standard-bearer for proper ownership in MLB, Walter is being investigated by the feds for potential loan fraud through his holding company, TWG Global. At the same time, he's the subject of multiple lawsuits, one of which is a class action suit alleging mishandling of client retirement funds. All of this may mean major fines, settlements, or judgments against Walter's interests. Walter has already sold his controlling share of the NBA's Lakers and his minority stake in Chelsea F.C. of the English Premier League. While the Dodgers insist Walter isn't putting the club up for sale, it's hard to trust what parties with vested interests say about such things. Even if Walter doesn't sell the Dodgers, it's entirely possible, maybe even likely, that his appetite for spending on player payroll will be diminished. And that's assuming he'll even be allowed to spend at such levels according to the terms of the next CBA. 
Never count an Andrew Friedman team out, of course, and the Dodgers aren't suddenly going to tumble to a win total in the seventies next season. They'll still probably be among the top quartile of MLB teams. However, their fading ability to dominate -- the Brewers had a better record and run differential against a tougher schedule this season -- looks poised to continue fading. That's a jarring reality for the team that's lorded over the sport for the last decade. But a reality it is.

title: 2026 WNBA Finals predictions: Expert picks for Valkyries vs. Dream as each team seeks first title - CBS Sports
description: The 2026 WNBA Finals tip off on Saturday afternoon ... so who will capture the championship?
body:
The 2026 WNBA Finals tip off on Saturday afternoon ... so who will capture the championship?
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:11 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The WNBA will have a first-time champion in 2026. The Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream are squaring off in the 2026 WNBA Finals, and neither franchise has ever won a title. The Valkyries are in just their second season after debuting as an expansion team in 2025. The Dream, meanwhile, have been to the WNBA Finals on three occasions (2010, 2011 and 2013) but have been swept each time.They both knocked out more-experienced teams to get here. The Valkyries took down the reigning champion Aces in the semis, while the Dream ousted the Liberty. So who will win a historic title in 2026? Before Game 1 on Saturday, our experts are making their predictions.2026 WNBA Finals predictions
                    
    
                                            
                    
                                    Lindsay Gibbs
                            
            
                    
    
                                            
                    
                                    Jack Maloney
                            
            2026 WNBA Finals pick
                            
    
                                                
                    
    
        
                            Dream
                    
    
    
                            
    
                                                
                    
    
        
                            Valkyries
                    
    
    Expert explanationsGibbs: Dream in 7. The Golden State Valkyries won the regular-season series over the Atlanta Dream 3-0, but that record doesn't quite tell the whole story. Two of those games were decided in the final minute, and all three of those meetings came in a 10-day span early in the season, with the Valkyries getting wins over the Dream on June 24, June 26 and July 4.
Those three losses were part of a five-game losing skid by the Dream, who sat at 12-9 on July 5.The Dream have only lost five games total since, finishing the regular season with an 18-5 run. Including the postseason, Atlanta has won 10 in a row and 14 of its last 15. In August and September, the Dream led the league in offense with a 115.2 rating and were second only to the Valkyries with a 100.8 defensive rating, both about five-point improvements on their early-season ratings. Simply put, this is a different Dream team than the one the Valkyries swept this summer.I can truly talk myself into either team winning this series – both are obviously in exceptional form and have been for the past three months, both feel like teams of destiny, both are trying to win the first title for their franchise and both are physical, dogged competitors who aren't afraid of winning ugly, which is a requirement for every title team.
The Valkyries are healthier and deeper than the Dream – the Allisha Gray injury is a big worry for Atlanta – and have home-court advantage. Defense wins championships, and the Valkyries have been far and away the best defense all season. And yet, I'm giving the Dream the edge. They have two players who have won WNBA titles in DeWanna Bonner and Jordin Canada, the far more potent offense and, while the Valkyries have the best defense, the Dream have the edge on the boards and in the paint.In the spirit of Angel Reese and Joe Lacob, I am manifesting an epic seven-game series full of twists and turns. And, at the end, it will be a big defensive play by Reese that will seal the title for the Dream on the road in front of a raucous Ballhalla crowd on Halloween night.
        
            
                From stunning Angel Reese trade to expansion ingenuity: How Dream, Valkyries broke the mold to reach Finals
                
                    Jack Maloney                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Maloney: Valkyries in 6. I wish that we had more clarity on Allisha Gray's injury, what procedure she had done and what she'll be able to give the Dream -- if she's even able to play at all. Both teams have similar styles and it's difficult to get a good feel on this matchup in the best of circumstances. The uncertainty surrounding Gray makes it nearly impossible.
It is safe to assume Gray will not be close to 100% if she does play, however, especially early in the series, and that's one of the reasons I'm going with the Valkyries. Gray led the Dream in scoring during the regular season at 19 points per game, which was good for ninth in the league, and was their go-to option late in games. Jordin Canada, DeWanna Bonner and Isobel Borlase were able to make up for Gray's production in the semifinals, but I'm not super confident they can continue to hit such incredible heights, especially against the best defense in the league.I'm going to crib here from an article I wrote about Gray's injury, which shows how incredible that trio was last round:Canada had three of the five-highest playoff scoring performances of her career against the Liberty, and averaged 22.3 points on 62.2/61.5/100 shooting splits -- up from 11.6 points on 43.1/29.2/78.2 shooting in the regular season. Bonner went for 15.3 points and 8.3 rebounds on 50/46.7/80 shooting splits, up from 10.4 points and six rebounds on 40.2/27.9/84.3 shooting between the Phoenix Mercury and Dream in the regular season. And Borlase, who only had six double-digit scoring games in the regular season, came off the bench to chip in 11 points in Game 2 and 10 points in Game 3 while shooting 9 of 15, including 3 of 6 from 3-point range. Of course, the counterpoint there is they may not have to be that good if Gray is back and Rhyne Howard doesn't shoot 31.1% from the field like she did against the Liberty. Regardless, I worry about the Dream's ability to generate consistent offense, especially with how reliant they are on forcing turnovers, and how good the Valkyries are at taking care of the ball. During the regular season, the Dream led the league in opponent turnover rate (19.5%) and points off turnovers (18.1), but the Valkyries were tied for second in turnover rate (15.1%) and first in opponent points off turnovers (11.7) by a wide margin.The Valkyries have plenty of their own offensive issues and regardless of Gray's status will have trouble scoring against a Dream defense that has been spectacular in the playoffs. Time and time and time again, however, the Valkyries have made it clear that they're not only capable of winning ugly, they prefer it that way.I also think the Valkyries' homecourt advantage will be a big factor in this series. The Valkyries were a league-best 17-5 at home during the regular season, and are 4-0 at Chase Center during the playoffs. Their defense, which was four points per 100 possessions than any other team this season, was even better at home, where they boasted a 98.2 defensive rating and a 19.7% opponent turnover rate. Ballhalla is the most raucous atmosphere in the league, and can cause opponents to spiral, as we've already seen this postseason. Plus, the Valkyries shot 36.1% from 3-point range at home, compared to 32.6% on the road. For a team that once again broke the record by taking 30.3 3s per game, that's a big deal.All told, I'm going Valkyries in 6 in what should be an extremely tough, physical and competitive series.

body:
Parker says he will "most likely" remain on the sideline, but the addition of Mike Pettine underscores the urgency in Dallas
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026
                            
                    at
    6:28 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        FRISCO, Texas -- Any football fan knows that when a coach or coordinator is moved up to the booth, it's the start of a performance improvement plan that typically does not end well.Jerry Jones said Tuesday on 105.3 The Fan that Christian Parker would move upstairs for Week 6. Parker himself pushed back on that notion on Thursday, saying he will "most likely" remain down on the sideline. "There's advantages of both for sure, but I've always been a guy that's usually been down on the field," Parker said. Parker also received the dreaded vote of confidence from Brian Schottenheimer amid his struggling defense's performance in the Cowboys' 2-3 start to the 2026 season. That came in the wake of Dallas hiring former Cleveland Browns coach Mike Pettine as a senior assistant. Pettine actually gave Parker his first job in the NFL when he was Green Bay's defensive coordinator in 2019.   
"Christian Parker is our defensive coordinator and everything, all decisions, will run through him," Schottenheimer said Wednesday. "We're supporting him. I support him. I believe so strongly in the guy. I do. I think the guy's an incredible football coach. We have to coach better. We got to play better. I think our players will be the first ones to say there's things that they need to do better. There's things I need to do better.  And so no one is sitting here pointing fingers at Christian Parker. But as the head coach, you have to make decisions that you think helps you win games. That's not just adding a Mike Pettine, it's some of the personnel adjustments that I know you guys are dying to know about that are being worked on behind the scenes and communicated to the players."Dallas knows that being the league's 31st-ranked total defense (395.4 total yards per game allowed), last-place run defense (168.4 rushing yards per game allowed) and worst third-down defense (52.6% third-down conversion rate allowed) won't cut it.How fixable are the issues? "Very fixable because they're under our control," Parker said. "Very fixable."The level of urgency Parker and his players have shown through five weeks is far from an overreaction. Matt Eberflus, Parker's predecessor in 2025, had the Dallas defense looking very similar through five weeks. The only significant difference is that Eberflus' unit was the league's worst against the pass, while Parker's is the league's worst against the run.

He played in 48.1% (25 of 52) of the Cowboys' defensive snaps in their 34-30 road win over the Houston Texans. He and the team were ramping up for him to be a full-time starter after being on the roster for a week, but he was scratched shortly before kickoff in Week 5 because he couldn't stop throwing up. Losing his No. 1 corner that close to kickoff was something Parker called "not ideal." However, he and Porter Jr. are ready for him to have a "heavily increased" workload against the Green Bay Packers.Look for rookie first-round edge rusher Malachi Lawrence to get more involved. Lawrence racked up his first career sack as well as a pass defensed in Week 5 against the Buccaneers. His quarterback pressure rate of 14.3% ranks fourth among qualified rookies, according to Pro Football Focus. He trails only David Bailey (16.4%), Sonny Styles (15%) and Cashius Howell (14.8%). Through five weeks, Lawrence co-leads the Cowboys in sacks with 1.0 despite playing significantly fewer pass rush snaps than some of Dallas' other edge rushers and defensive linemen. "Played very well," Schottenheimer said. "I think he's starting to show the flash and the acceleration and the ability to rush the passer that we knew we were getting when we drafted him. And I thought he had a very, very good game against Tampa Bay and you'll see him get more opps [opportunities]."    Cowboys pass rush snap leaders this seasonDefensive snaps as pass rusher  SacksQB pressure rateDT Quinnen Williams1211.010.7%DT Kenny Clark1110.06.3%OLB Donovan Ezeiruaku     1060.59.4%OLB Rashan Gary 1011.014.9%DT Otito Ogbonnia  570.07%OLB Malachi Lawrence491.014.3%DT LT Overton390.05.1%OLB Von Miller360.016.7%DT Jonathan Bullard210.59.5%LB Jaishawn Barham110.027.3%They'll need Lawrence to beat Packers left tackle Jordan Morgan with regularity to have any hope of slowing down Green Bay quarterback Jordan Love and his top two speedy receivers, Christian Watson and Matthew Golden. Dallas sees facing a high-powered Packers passing attack as an opportunity rather than a challenge. "I see that we have a lot of opportunities to make plays on the ball, so I know we're all excited for that," Porter Jr. said. "We really have to rally to the ball and make plays when they call on us to."
